## NVIDIA Fiscal 2024 10-K (FY ended January 28, 2024) — Inventory-related charges to cost of revenue

**Source document:** `NVDA_2024_10K.pdf`

### 1. Total provisions: $2.2 billion (MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p. 40)
> "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled **$2.2 billion** for both fiscal years 2024 and 2023."

This is the combined fiscal 2024 charge to cost of revenue and comprises the two components below.

### 2. Component A — Inventory provision (excess/obsolete inventory write-down): $774 million
*(Note 10 – Balance Sheet Components, footnote (1) to Inventories, p. 68)*
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an **inventory provision of $774 million** and $1.0 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue."

This is the write-down of inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value for excess or obsolete quantities (i.e., excess quantities of products or components, based on inventory levels and purchase commitments versus assumptions about future demand and market conditions).

### 3. Component B — Excess inventory purchase obligations: approximately $1.4 billion
*(Note 10 – Balance Sheet Components, footnote (1) to "Excess inventory purchase obligations" within Accrued and Other Current Liabilities, p. 70)*
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an expense of **approximately $1.4 billion** and $1.1 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue for **inventory purchase obligations in excess of our current demand projections, supplier charges and for penalties related to cancellations and underutilization**."

Component B is an expense (not a balance-sheet inventory write-down) covering non-cancellable supplier purchase commitments in excess of demand forecasts, plus related supplier charges and cancellation/underutilization penalties.

*(Note the rounding: $774 million + ~$1.4 billion ≈ the $2.2 billion total quoted in MD&A.)*

### 4. Provision releases: $540 million (MD&A, p. 40)
> "Sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations resulted in a **provision release of $540 million** ... for fiscal years 2024."

This release is the credit to cost of revenue arising from (a) selling inventory that had previously been written down/reserved, and (b) settling excess inventory purchase obligations. Once written down, inventory creates a new cost basis and is not written back up (Note 1, Inventories policy, p. 58).

### Net effect
Net fiscal 2024 inventory-related charge to cost of revenue = $2.2 billion of provisions less $540 million of releases ≈ **$1.66 billion net**.

### Supporting context (no additional fiscal 2024 charge amounts disclosed)
- Note 1 (Inventories policy, p. 58): "We charge cost of sales for inventory provisions to write-down our inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value or for obsolete or excess inventory, and for excess product purchase commitments... We record a liability for noncancelable purchase commitments with suppliers for quantities in excess of our future demand forecasts consistent with our valuation of obsolete or excess inventory."
- PwC's critical audit matter (p. 49) is "Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments," reflecting the judgment involved in these estimates; the dollar figures cited there ($5.3 billion inventories; $16.1 billion inventory purchase and long-term supply/capacity obligations) are year-end balances, not fiscal 2024 charges, and are excluded per your instruction.

**Excluded as requested:** year-end balances (excess inventory purchase obligations of $1,655 million; total inventories $5,282 million; $16.1 billion purchase and capacity obligations; $2.5 billion short-term prepaid supply and capacity agreements), the 2.7% gross margin impact, and all fiscal 2023 comparatives ($1.0 billion inventory provision, $1.1 billion purchase obligation expense, $137 million release).

Based on Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (`AAPL_2024_10K.pdf`), four reported fiscal 2024 results (vs. fiscal 2023) were unfavorably affected by weakness of foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar:

**1. Greater China net sales — currency: renminbi**
> "Greater China net sales decreased during 2024 compared to 2023 due primarily to lower net sales of iPhone and iPad. The weakness in the renminbi relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Greater China net sales during 2024."
Net sales fell 8% to $66,952M (from $72,559M) — the only segment whose sales actually declined. (Item 7, p. 22 of the 10-K)

**2. Japan net sales — currency: yen**
> "Japan net sales increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due primarily to higher net sales of iPhone. The weakness in the yen relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Japan net sales during 2024."
Net sales rose 3% to $25,052M (from $24,257M) — i.e., currency was a drag on the increase, not a driver of a decline. (Item 7, p. 22)

**3. Rest of Asia Pacific net sales — currency: foreign currencies generally (no single currency named)**
> "Rest of Asia Pacific net sales increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due primarily to higher net sales of Services. The weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar had a net unfavorable year-over-year impact on Rest of Asia Pacific net sales during 2024."
Net sales rose 4% to $30,658M (from $29,615M). (Item 7, p. 22)

**4. Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage**
> "Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage increased during 2024 compared to 3 due to cost savings, partially offset by a different Products mix and the weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar."
Products gross margin was $109,633M (37.2%) vs. $108,803M (36.5%) in 2023 — currency weakness partially offset the cost savings and mix benefits. (Item 7, p. 24)

**Notable exclusions (no currency attribution):**
- Americas and Europe net sales, and iPhone/Mac/iPad/Wearables/Services net sales by category — no currency effect cited.
- Services gross margin, operating expenses (R&D, SG&A), and the effective tax rate (24.1% in 2024) — currency is not cited as a factor.
- Item 7A and the risk factors address currency only generically (a strengthening U.S. dollar negatively affects net sales and gross margins; hedging may offset only a portion), not as a 2024-specific driver.

One nuance worth flagging: for Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific, currency weakness reduced the *year-over-year change* in net sales in regions where sales still grew; only Greater China saw an actual sales decline.

| **Total fiscal 2026 goodwill added** | **$15.6 billion** | All allocated to the Compute & Networking reporting unit; no goodwill was added to Graphics (Graphics goodwill was unchanged at $370 million). |

### Supporting context

- MD&A confirms investing cash outflow was "driven by higher purchases of equity investment securities and the execution of a non-exclusive license agreement with Groq" (page 43).

**Excluded as requested:** the $5,188 million ($5.2 billion) goodwill balance at January 26, 2025, and its split of $4.8 billion (Compute & Networking) / $370 million (Graphics).

Walmart's fiscal 2022 Form 10-K (FY ended January 31, 2022) gives pickup and delivery location counts in three places — one company-wide figure and one for each of the two retail segments:

### 1. Company-wide (all segments, global) — Item 1, "The Development of Our Company" (p. 6)

> "In 2007, leveraging our physical stores, walmart.com launched its Site to Store service, enabling customers to make a purchase online and pick up merchandise in stores. **To date, we now have over 8,000 pickup and 6,000 delivery locations globally.**"

- **Business:** the whole company's eCommerce/omnichannel operation (Walmart U.S., Walmart International and Sam's Club combined).
- **Service:** pickup (e.g., Site to Store) and delivery to customers.
- **Qualifiers:** pickup — "over 8,000"; delivery — "6,000" (no "over"/"approximately" on the delivery figure).

### 2. Walmart U.S. segment — "Omni-channel" (p. 7)

> "**As of January 31, 2022, we had approximately 4,600 pickup locations and more than 3,500 same-day delivery locations.**"

- **Business:** the Walmart U.S. segment (U.S., all 50 states, Washington D.C. and Puerto Rico), described in the "Omni-channel" discussion alongside pickup, delivery, ship-from-store and digital pharmacy fulfillment.
- **Service:** the delivery count is specifically **same-day delivery**.
- **Qualifiers:** pickup — "approximately 4,600"; delivery — "more than 3,500."

### 3. Walmart International segment — "Omni-channel" (p. 9)

> "**As of January 31, 2022, Walmart International had approximately 2,900 pickup and over 1,900 delivery locations.**"

- **Business:** the Walmart International segment (23 countries outside the U.S.).
- **Service:** pickup and delivery in international markets (the surrounding text discusses pickup and delivery services in most markets, same-day delivery expansion in Mexico, and one-hour delivery in China via JD.com).
- **Qualifiers:** pickup — "approximately 2,900"; delivery — "over 1,900."

### Notes / caveats

- **Sam's Club segment:** the filing gives **no pickup or delivery location counts** for this segment. It only states that Curbside Pickup is available at all clubs and describes ship-from-club and delivery-from-club (p. 10). This is why the global "over 8,000 / 6,000" figures exceed the sum of the two disclosed segment counts (approx. 7,500 pickup; 5,400 delivery).
- **Not to be confused with** the facility counts the filing gives elsewhere: 31 dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers and 157 distribution facilities (Walmart U.S.), 83 eCommerce fulfillment centers, 179 distribution facilities and "more than 3,400 eCommerce sort centers and last-mile delivery facilities in India" (Walmart International), and 12 eCommerce fulfillment centers / 28 distribution facilities (Sam's Club). These are distribution, fulfillment and sort facilities, not customer pickup or delivery locations.
- The filing also says Walmart U.S. can "ship or deliver directly from more than 3,500 stores" (p. 8) — a store count used in the distribution discussion, not a delivery-location count.

## What these swaps do

Per Note 1 (Cash Flow Hedges, page 61), Walmart is a party to receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency interest rate swaps used to hedge the currency exposure associated with the **forecasted payments of principal and interest of certain non-U.S.-denominated debt**. NVIDIA's FY2023 Form 10-K (fiscal year ended January 29, 2023) addresses the Ukraine war and the resulting sanctions in two places: the risk factor "Our operations could be affected by the complex laws, rules and regulations to which our business is subject..." (Item 1A, p. 28) and the MD&A subsection captioned "Russia" (Item 7, p. 37).

## Effects the filing says occurred (or may have occurred) in fiscal 2023

1. **Products, services and support were blocked from Russia, Belarus and certain regions of Ukraine.** The filing states: "in response to the war in Ukraine, the United States and other jurisdictions imposed economic sanctions and export control measures which blocked the passage of our products, services and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine." (p. 28) The block covered services and support, not just hardware.

2. **NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2023.** (p. 28 and p. 37)

3. **NVIDIA closed its business operations in Russia.** The MD&A adds the sequencing: "In fiscal year 2023, we stopped direct sales to Russia and later in the year, we closed business operations in Russia." (p. 37)

4. **The revenue significance of that exit was immaterial.** "Direct sales to Russia in fiscal year 2022 were immaterial." (p. 37) Consistently with this, Note 17's revenue-by-geography table (p. 85) shows no separate Russia line, and Russia is buried in "Other countries" ($5,911M in FY2023 vs. $6,910M in FY2022).

5. **The war impacted end-customer sales in EMEA.** Stated in the present perfect — "the war in Ukraine has impacted end customer sales in EMEA" — with the added caveat that it "may continue to do so in the future." (p. 28)

6. **Revenue to partners who sell into Russia may have been negatively impacted.** MD&A: "Our revenue to partners that sell into Russia may have been negatively impacted due to the war in Ukraine." (p. 37) This is the filing's only "may have happened" effect, and it is distinct from direct sales, which NVIDIA ended outright.

## The export-control regime in which those Russia restrictions sit

The Ukraine-related measures operated inside the broader license regime NVIDIA describes (MD&A "Global Trade," p. 37; Item 1A, pp. 28–29; Item 1 "Government Regulations," p. 11). In the third quarter of fiscal 2023 the U.S. government announced new license requirements covering exports to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) **and Russia** of the A100 and H100 integrated circuits, DGX and other systems or boards incorporating those chips, and the A100X. Effects NVIDIA describes as already in effect:

- **Management burden and forecasting difficulty:** "The impact of the new license requirements is difficult to quantify, and it may be challenging for us to manage our operations and forecast our operating results due to these requirements" (p. 11); "Management of these new license and other requirements is complicated and time consuming" (p. 37).
- **Required relocation of operations out of China, at cost and with revenue disruption:** "We are required to transition certain operations out of China (including Hong Kong), which could be costly and time consuming, and adversely affect our research and development and supply and distribution operations, as well as our revenue, during any such transition period." (p. 29)
- **A product response (A800) for China, with associated risks** of customer rejection, substitution to competitors or in-house solutions, license delays/denials, transition costs, and excess inventory (pp. 29, 37).
- **Chinese government restrictions** on gaming activity and increased oversight of digital platform companies, affecting Gaming and Data Center revenue (p. 29).

Note the filing attributes the A100/H100 license regime to rules targeting "China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries" (p. 29), not to the Ukraine response; only the Russia/Belarus/Ukraine-region block is expressly tied to the war.

## Excluded as forward-looking only (per your instruction)

The filing's purely prospective statements on this subject — and therefore not counted as effects that occurred or may have occurred — include: the war's EMEA impact "may continue to do so in the future"; "Increasing use of economic sanctions may also impact demand for our products or services"; the risk of penalties if NVIDIA were found to have violated export control laws or sanctions "even if the violation occurred without our knowledge"; the prospect of additional unilateral or multilateral AI/AI-chip export controls, retaliatory foreign measures, deemed-export limitations and R&D roadmap delays; and the listed China-specific harm scenarios (customer refusal of A800, license denial, excess inventory) which NVIDIA frames as "may be harmed if." (pp. 28–29)

One adjacent item is generic rather than Ukraine-specific: the filing notes heightened cyber-attack risk "during times of war or other major conflicts" and that acts of war or military actions generally could disrupt operations (pp. 22–24), but it does not attribute any actual cyber or business-disruption event to the Ukraine war.

**2. The specific factors management considered.** The MD&A enumerates them: "announcements by airlines concerning potential future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders, announcements by manufacturers of reduced aircraft production, and the actions we were taking or may be taking in the future to restructure operations."

**3. So the charges were driven by two assumption changes: higher discount rates and lower long-term cash flow forecasts. **4. The filing also repeatedly emphasizes the inherent subjectivity: "Significant judgment is required in estimating the fair value of a reporting unit and in performing impairment tests. Due to the inherent uncertainty in forecasting future cash flows and earnings, actual results in the future may vary significantly from the forecasts."

**6. Corroborating business conditions disclosed for PCC (MD&A, Industrial products).** PCC's 2020 revenues fell 28.9% to $7.3 billion and pre-tax earnings fell 64.5% to $650 million. **8. **1. No readily determinable fair value / no active market**
- Note 1 (Significant Accounting Policies, p. 60): "Non-marketable equity securities consist of investments in privately-held companies that do not have a readily determinable fair value." Because there is no active market, "fair value is based upon observable inputs in an inactive market."
- Critical Accounting Estimates (p. 38): these are "investments in private companies without readily determinable fair values."

**2. Absence of market prices and lack of liquidity**
- Note 1 (p. 60) states expressly that "the valuation requires our judgment due to the absence of market prices and inherent lack of liquidity." In effect, these are Level 3 measurements — per the Note 1 fair value hierarchy (p. 59), Level 3 means "unobservable inputs in which there is little or no market data that are significant to the fair value of the assets or liabilities."

**3. Lack of readily available market data and observable transactions, plus macroeconomic effects**
- Item 7A, Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk (p. 45): "Valuations of our non-marketable equity securities are inherently complex due to the lack of readily available market data and observable transactions, and impact of macroeconomic factors."

**4. Reliance on unobservable inputs in the valuation models**
- Because observable inputs are limited, the measurement alternative requires judgment. Note 8 (p. 66) describes valuations "applying valuation methods based on observable transactions for similar investments of the same issuer and unobservable inputs such as volatility, expected time to liquidity, risk free rate and security-specific rights and obligations."
- Critical Accounting Estimates (p. 38) similarly notes that adjustments for observable price changes in orderly transactions for a similar investment in the same issuer (the measurement alternative) "may require use of unobservable inputs."

**5. Subjective, forward-looking impairment assessment**
- The carrying amounts depend on a recurring impairment judgment: NVIDIA "assesses impairment quarterly based on qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee's operating performance and market trends" (p. 38), and in Note 1 it assesses impairment "based on quantitative and qualitative factors," writing the investment down to fair value with the charge recorded in Other income, net (p. 60).

**6. The measurement alternative and related method changes create judgment around transitions**
- Under the measurement alternative, the investments are carried at cost minus impairment and adjusted only for observable price changes in orderly transactions for an identical or similar investment in the same issuer. Because a position can begin trading publicly and be reclassified to marketable securities (Note 8 shows $848 million of such reclassifications in fiscal 2026), the valuation method for a given holding changes over time, requiring judgment about when and how to apply it.

## Where the numbers come from

Note 10A (Identifiable Intangible Assets) of Pfizer's 2025 Form 10-K shows IPR&D — an indefinite-lived asset, so it is carried at gross amount with no amortization — rising from **$18,893 million at December 31, 2024 to $21,760 million at December 31, 2025** (a $2,867 million increase).

## Causes of the increase

**1. The Metsera acquisition (the dominant driver).** Note 10 states that the increase in gross carrying amount "primarily reflects $8.0 billion for the acquisition of Metsera (see Note 2A), partially offset by impairments of $3.9 billion (see Note 4) and the transfers to developed technology rights noted above." Note 2A explains that on November 13, 2025 Pfizer acquired Metsera, a clinical-stage company in obesity and cardiometabolic disease, for $65.60 per share in cash plus a CVR of up to $20.65 per share (up to $2.3 billion) tied to three milestones (Phase 3 start of the MET-097i+MET-233i combination, and FDA approval of MET-097i monotherapy and of the combination). Total fair value of consideration transferred was $8.0 billion ($7.8 billion net of cash acquired), including $632 million for the non-cash CVRs and $475 million for employee stock awards for pre-acquisition service. Pfizer "provisionally recorded (i) $8.0 billion of identifiable intangible assets, net, consisting of IPR&D," together with $2.2 billion of goodwill, $1.7 billion of net deferred tax liabilities and a $635 million contingent consideration liability assumed from Metsera. The allocation is provisional and subject to change. The Metsera assets (MET-097i+MET-233i combination and MET-097i monotherapy) are now among the "significant components of IPR&D" listed in Note 10.

**2. Foreign exchange.** Note 10 cites the impact of foreign exchange as an element of the changes in gross carrying amounts in the intangible asset table (explicitly for developed technology rights). For IPR&D this effect is small — the arithmetic (18,893 + 8,000 − 3,903 − 1,190 = 21,800) leaves only about $40 million of residual FX/other.

## The offsets

**1. $3.9 billion of IPR&D impairment charges.** Note 4 reports 2025 "Certain asset impairments" of **$4,940 million** (vs. $3,295 million in 2024 and $3,024 million in 2023), all in the Biopharma segment, "primarily due to changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts." These comprise (i) **$3.9 billion of IPR&D impairments** — primarily $1.6 billion for **disitamab vedotin**, $820 million for **Tukysa (tucatinib)** and $820 million for **osivelotor** — and (ii) $1.0 billion of impairments primarily for certain U.S. sterile injectable and hospital products (i.e., not IPR&D). Per the Note 4 table, the impaired IPR&D ($3,903 million) was written down to a remaining fair value of $4,400 million (all Level 3), determined using the income approach (multi-period excess earnings / discounted cash flow), with key assumptions being the amount and timing of projected net cash flows, probability of technical and regulatory success (PTRS) of ongoing clinical trials, the discount rate and the tax rate. The $1.6 billion increase in impairment charges was one of the drivers of the $503 million decline in 2025 pretax income from continuing operations.

**2. Transfers out of IPR&D into developed technology rights upon approval.** Note 10 records transfers of **$600 million (Padcev)** and **$590 million (talazoparib/Talzenna)** from IPR&D to developed technology rights. Once an asset is approved in a major market, Pfizer determines a useful life, reclassifies it out of IPR&D and begins amortizing it, so approved programs leave the IPR&D balance (this also contributed to the $413 million decline in amortization expense, alongside Prevnar and fully amortized assets).

**3. A point worth noting:** Pfizer's two 2025 in-licensing deals (3SBio, $1.25 billion upfront plus a $100 million option payment and a $100 million equity investment, and YaoPharma, $150 million upfront) did **not** add to the IPR&D asset balance — they were expensed as Acquired in-process research and development expenses ($1.35 billion and $150 million), because pre-approval upfront and milestone payments for IP rights are expensed rather than capitalized.

## Why Pfizer flags IPR&D as its most impairment-prone asset

The MD&A critical accounting estimates (Asset Impairments) note that IPR&D assets of approximately $21.8 billion at December 31, 2025 are the assets "most at risk of impairment" because R&D is high-risk and uncertain; they are tested at least annually, and if the associated R&D effort is abandoned the related IPR&D is written off with an impairment charge. The impairment indicators Pfizer lists include changes in development plans and/or de-prioritization of assets, expectation of reduced profits, a change in outlook based on clinical trial data, a delay in projected launch dates, additional commercialization expenditures, and competitive or legal/regulatory forces. The risk factors similarly state that IPR&D "have and may become impaired and/or be written off in the future if the associated R&D effort is abandoned or is curtailed." The specific development-plan changes behind the 2025 charges are visible elsewhere in the filing: Pfizer removed the first-line HER2+ metastatic breast cancer program for Tukysa from its late-stage development table; osivelotor remained under an FDA partial clinical hold from December 2024 (with new enrollment only expected to begin in the first quarter of 2026); and the sasanlimab filing was withdrawn in the U.S. in December 2025 and in the EU in February 2026 to allow more time for data collection.

**In short:** the increase is principally the $8.0 billion of IPR&D recognized on the Metsera acquisition (plus a small FX effect), partially offset by $3.9 billion of IPR&D impairments driven by changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts (disitamab vedotin, Tukysa and osivelotor being the largest) and by $1.19 billion of approved assets (Padcev and Talzenna) being reclassified out of IPR&D into amortizable developed technology rights.

**The delivery decline.** In Item 7 (MD&A), Commercial Airplanes deliveries (including intercompany) fell from **528 airplanes in 2023 to 348 in 2024**, with every model down: 737 from 396 to 265, 767 from 32 to 18, 777 from 26 to 14, 787 from 73 to 51, and 747 from 1 to 0 (the 747 program ended production in Q4 2022, with final delivery in February 2023 — the filing presents this as program completion, not as a delivery driver).

**Causes the filing links to deliveries (six):**

1. **The IAM 751 work stoppage.** The MD&A Overview states this directly: "The IAM 751 work stoppage significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024." The strike began September 13, 2024 and ended with ratification on November 4, with production resuming in December, so the pause fell entirely in 2H 2024. The 10-K again names the work stoppage as a driver of "lower deliveries" in the Cash Flow Summary and in Capital Resources.

2. **Safety and quality actions following the January 5, 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 door-plug accident.** In the Cash Flow Summary, Boeing says commercial airplane "cash outflows reflect slowed and/or paused production and **lower deliveries as a result of ongoing safety and quality improvement actions the Company is taking following the Alaska Airlines accident**." The FAA grounded the 737-9 fleet; all 737-9 aircraft in production had to undergo the enhanced inspection process before delivery; the FAA said it would not approve 737 rate increases above 38 per month or additional production lines until quality and safety standards were met; and Boeing slowed rates and delayed planned rate increases under its safety and quality plan.

3. **Supply chain constraints and disruptions.** Named alongside the safety/quality actions and the strike as a cause of "lower deliveries" in the Cash Flow Summary and Capital Resources. Management attributes these to supplier quality problems, global supply chain constraints, labor instability and inflation, with 767 factory disruption (supply chain delays and quality issues) and 787 production slowed below 5 per month.

4. **787 business-class seat delays.** "Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025." Separately, about 25 pre-2023 787s sat in inventory requiring rework, with the majority expected to be delivered in 2025.

5. **777X flight-test and certification delays.** Certification flight testing was paused from August; the first 777-9 delivery slipped to 2026 and the 777-8 Freighter to 2028 (777-8 passenger not before 2030); and slowing the 777X rate ramp "resulted in higher production costs and **further customer delivery delays**." 777 deliveries fell from 26 to 14.

6. **737-7 and 737-10 certification delays.** Certification was delayed while Boeing worked through the engine anti-ice engineering solution, leaving roughly 35 737-7/-10 aircraft in inventory at year-end whose delivery is deferred to 2025. About 55 built 737-8s (including roughly 40 for Chinese customers) were also held for 2025 delivery. The filing's delivery link here is the undeliverable inventory plus the risk-factor statement that "delays on the 737, 777X and 787 programs have resulted in ... customers having the right to terminate orders, be compensated for late deliveries and/or substitute orders."

**Causes excluded under your instruction** (given only for production rates, costs, or revenue, not deliveries): the 737 cap of 38 per month and delayed rate increases and the slowed 777X ramp as rate actions; the $4.079 billion of 777X and 767 reach-forward losses, the 767 accounting-quantity reductions, and the decision to end 767 freighter production in 2027; the $443 million of 737-9 customer considerations and 737 MAX concessions (revenue/liability effects, cited separately from deliveries in the revenue discussion); the new IAM 751 contract and pay enhancements and higher R&D (costs/margins); abnormal production cost changes; and general inflation, tariffs, Spirit AeroSystems and U.S. government funding items.

So the count is **six** causes that the 2024 10-K explicitly ties to lower commercial airplane deliveries.

**Higher mix of Data Center revenue.** The 10-K states: "Gross margins increased to 75.0% in fiscal year 2025 from 72.7% in fiscal year 2024. Data Center growth was driven by the Hopper architecture, with production Blackwell systems shipping in the fourth quarter.

### Unfavorable factor

**Inventory provisions and excess inventory purchase obligations.** The 10-K discloses: "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $3.7 billion and $2.2 billion for fiscal years 2025 and 2024, respectively. Because the gross drag from inventory was 2.3 points versus 2.7 points in fiscal 2024, this headwind was roughly 0.4 points *less* unfavorable year over year, contributing favorably to the net margin expansion.

### Related factors and context the 10-K identifies

- **Cost of revenue composition.** Gross profit is net revenue less cost of revenue, which "consists primarily of the cost of semiconductors, including wafer fabrication, assembly, testing and packaging, board and device costs, manufacturing support costs, including labor and overhead associated with such purchases, final test yield fallout, inventory and warranty provisions, memory and component costs, tariffs, and shipping costs. - **Macroeconomic factors.** Inflation, interest rate changes, capital market volatility, global supply chain constraints, tariffs, and global economic and geopolitical developments "impact our supply chain and manufacturing costs," though "our product and solution pricing generally does not fluctuate with short-term changes in our costs."
- **Product transitions and Blackwell ramp.** The 10-K explains that "we often ship both new and prior architecture products simultaneously," and that "the increased frequency and complexity of newly introduced products could result in quality or production issues that could increase inventory provisions, warranty, or other costs." - **Acquisition-related intangible amortization.** Amortization expense of intangibles included in cost of revenue was $593 million in fiscal 2025 versus $614 million in fiscal 2024 (Note 6) — a modest favorable.
- **Stock-based compensation in cost of revenue.** $178 million in fiscal 2025 versus $141 million in fiscal 2024 (Note 3) — a modest unfavorable, though small relative to revenue.
- **Supply and capacity commitments.** Purchase obligations reached $45.079 billion as of January 26, 2025, including $30.8 billion of inventory purchases and long-term supply/capacity agreements, up largely due to new product introductions including Blackwell, with $10.9 billion of multi-year cloud service agreements; some agreements can be canceled, rescheduled, or adjusted before firm orders "potentially at additional cost." NVIDIA also notes it may place non-cancellable inventory orders in advance of historical lead times and "pay premiums and provide deposits to secure future supply and capacity."
- **Export controls / China.** U.S. licensing requirements restrict exports of A100/H100/Blackwell products to China and other Country Groups; NVIDIA has not received licenses to ship restricted products to China, though China Data Center revenue grew in fiscal 2025 (still well below pre-October 2023 levels).
